questions.q: You are writing a new network application. On which devices do you need to write and run your application's software?
choices: Only on the end systems that run the application, such as the client and server hosts
On the end systems and on every router along the path between them
Only on the routers in the network core, which forward the application's messages
On the link-layer switches, which must parse each application message
questions.explain: Network applications are programs that run on (different) end systems and communicate over the network, e.g., web server software talking to browser software. Network-core devices such as routers do not run user applications, so you never write software for them.

questions.q: Because network-core devices do not run user applications, a new application can be deployed without changing any routers, which allows rapid app development and propagation.
questions.explain: Keeping applications on end systems means only the hosts running the app need new software. That is why new applications can be developed and spread quickly.

questions.q: Which description of a network application matches the lecture?
choices: A single program that is compiled and run on one host
A distributed set of interacting processes, on different end systems, that exchange messages
A set of forwarding rules installed in the routers of the network core
An operating-system service for inter-process communication within one host
questions.explain: A network application is not one standalone program. It is several programs (client/server or peers) running as processes on different hosts and exchanging messages.

questions.q: Writing a network application is easier than it sounds because the complexity inside the network can be abstracted away. Which two things does the developer mainly need to understand?
choices: What services the transport layer provides
How the socket API gives the application access to those transport services
How routers in the network core compute their forwarding tables
How bits are encoded as signals on each physical link along the path
questions.explain: The application can only do what the transport layer's services allow, and it reaches those services through the socket API. Everything below (network, link, physical) is hidden from the developer.

questions.q: Ray Tomlinson's network email needed an address that named both the user and the machine the user was on. Why did he choose the @ sign as the separator?
choices: The ARPANET routing protocol required @ to mark a destination host
It was the only character that could be sent over the network without encoding
It was a keyboard character not already used by operating systems, and it reads naturally as user at host
The designers of the World Wide Web later picked it to link email addresses to web pages
questions.explain: Tomlinson had to separate the user's identity from the machine's identity. @ was the one keyboard character the operating systems weren't already using, and user@host reads as user at host.

questions.q: According to Vint Cerf, what lets people build new applications, such as smartphone apps, without knowing how the layers beneath them work?
choices: Requiring every developer to understand each layer down to the physical link
Patents on the core protocols, so one company wrote all the applications
Building each new application directly into the routers of the network core
Stable, long-lived interfaces, such as protocol interfaces and APIs, that isolate knowledge of the lower layers
questions.explain: Layering and abstraction: HTTP sits on TCP, and phone APIs sit on top of the mobile system. Because these interfaces are stable and last a long time, developers can invent new things without knowing much, if anything, about what lies underneath. Cerf also notes that the Internet's design was deliberately offered free, without patents, to encourage adoption.

questions.q: Most of today's popular network applications, such as social media, video streaming and video conferencing, were developed long after the Internet's layered architecture and transport-layer abstractions were defined.
questions.explain: Except for things like email and remote login, today's applications came much later. The architecture supported applications its designers could not have imagined, which suggests the layered design and abstractions were well chosen.

questions.q: Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web at CERN drew little attention at first. What made the general public notice it?
choices: The Mosaic graphical browser from NCSA, which showed pages like a magazine, with formatted text and images
The invention of network email at BBN
The introduction of UDP as an alternative to TCP
The opening of the first commercial packet-switch vendors
questions.explain: Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications built Mosaic, a graphical browser. It made the Web look like a magazine, so it got widely noticed, and the general public could easily publish and find content.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a server in the client-server paradigm?
choices: A host that is connected only some of the time and gets a new IP address each time
An always-on host with a permanent IP address
A host that only requests services and never provides them
Any end system that happens to be online at the moment
questions.explain: A server is an always-on host with a permanent IP address. It is often placed in a data center for scaling, but it can also run at a home, company or university.

questions.q: Which of the following are true of clients in the client-server paradigm?
choices: They contact and communicate with a server
They may be intermittently connected
They may have dynamic IP addresses
They communicate directly with other clients
They must have a permanent IP address so servers can find them
questions.explain: Clients contact the server, may be connected only some of the time (e.g., a phone or laptop), and may have dynamic IP addresses. They do not communicate directly with each other. Instead, they interact through the server.

questions.q: In the client-server paradigm, two clients (for example, two web browsers) communicate directly with each other.
questions.explain: Clients do not communicate directly with each other. Each client communicates with the server.

questions.q: Why does a server in the client-server paradigm have a permanent IP address?
choices: So that clients know where to contact it
So that it can exchange messages with other servers only
Because TCP refuses connections from hosts with dynamic addresses
So that it can run without a transport layer
questions.explain: Clients start the communication, so they need a fixed, known address for the always-on server they want to reach.

questions.q: Why are servers often placed in data centers?
choices: Because a server can only run inside a commercial data center
So that clients in the data center can talk directly to each other
For scaling, so the service can handle requests from very many clients
Because hosts in data centers never need an IP address
questions.explain: Data centers are used for scaling. A server can still run at a home, company or university. The data center just makes it possible to serve huge numbers of clients.

questions.q: Which of these are examples of client-server protocols?
choices: HTTP
IMAP
FTP
BitTorrent file sharing
questions.explain: HTTP (browser to web server), IMAP and FTP are client-server protocols. BitTorrent is the standard example of a P2P architecture.

questions.q: Which statement describes a peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture?
choices: All peers contact a single always-on server that relays their messages
Peers have permanent IP addresses so others can always find them
Peers only request services and never provide them
There is no always-on server, and arbitrary end systems communicate directly
questions.explain: P2P has no always-on server. Arbitrary end systems (peers) talk directly to each other, requesting services from other peers and providing services to them in return.

questions.q: In a P2P file-sharing system such as BitTorrent, what does a typical peer do?
choices: Requests files from other peers and also provides files to other peers
Downloads files only from one central always-on server
Only uploads files and never downloads them
Forwards other peers' packets like a router, without requesting anything itself
questions.explain: Peers both request services from other peers and provide services to them in return. In file sharing, a peer downloads from other peers and uploads to them.

questions.q: In a P2P architecture, each new peer brings new service capacity as well as new service demands. What is this property called?
questions.explain: Self scalability: as peers join, they add to the demand, and they also add capacity because they serve other peers.

questions.q: Why is managing a P2P application more complex than managing a client-server application?
choices: Every peer must be located in the same data center
Peers are intermittently connected and change IP addresses
Peers cannot create sockets
P2P applications are not allowed to use a transport layer
questions.explain: Peers come and go and their IP addresses change. Keeping track of who is available, and where, is much harder than contacting one always-on server at a permanent address.

questions.q: In the context of network applications, what is a process?
choices: A program running within a host
A message sent between two hosts
A router's forwarding table entry
A transport-layer connection between two sockets
questions.explain: A process is the running instance of a program on a host. Processes are what actually communicate in a network application.

questions.q: How do two processes communicate?
choices: Within one host, they must exchange messages over the Internet. Across hosts, they use the OS's inter-process communication.
Within one host, they use inter-process communication defined by the OS. Across hosts, they exchange messages over the network.
Both within one host and across hosts, they use inter-process communication defined by the OS.
They can only communicate if they run on different hosts.
questions.explain: On the same host, processes use inter-process communication (IPC), which the operating system defines. Processes on different hosts communicate by exchanging messages across the network, and that is the case network applications care about.

questions.q: When two processes start a communication session, which one is called the client process?
choices: The one that waits to be contacted
The one with more data to send
The one that initiates the communication
The one running on an always-on host in a data center
questions.explain: The client process initiates communication. The server process waits to be contacted. The roles depend on who starts the session, not on the type of host.

questions.q: Applications with P2P architectures have no client processes or server processes, because all peers are equal.
questions.explain: P2P applications still have client processes and server processes. In any given exchange, the peer that initiates communication acts as the client and the peer that is contacted acts as the server.

questions.q: A socket is often compared to a door. Using that analogy, what happens when a process sends a message?
choices: The process routes the message hop by hop to the destination host itself
The operating system hands the message straight to the receiving application, skipping its socket
The message waits behind the door until the receiving process walks over and fetches it
The process shoves the message out its socket and relies on the transport infrastructure on the other side to deliver it to the receiving process's socket
questions.explain: The process just pushes the message out its door (socket). Delivering it to the socket at the receiving process is up to the transport, network and link layers on the other side of the door.

questions.q: How many sockets are involved when a sending process communicates with a receiving process?
questions.explain: Two sockets are involved, one on each side of the communication: one at the sending process and one at the receiving process.

questions.q: In a host's protocol stack, which part is controlled by the application developer?
choices: The application process, on the application side of the socket
The transport layer and everything below it
Only the network and link layers
The whole stack, from the application down to the physical layer
questions.explain: The developer controls the application process above the socket. The transport, network, link and physical layers below the socket are controlled by the operating system.

questions.q: A process sends messages into the network and receives messages from it through a software interface that is often compared to a door. What is this interface called?
questions.explain: The socket is the interface between the application process and the transport layer. It is the main abstraction the Internet uses for communication between processes.

questions.q: The IP address of the host a process runs on is enough to identify that process.
questions.explain: Many processes can run on the same host, so the IP address alone cannot tell them apart. A port number is also needed.

questions.q: To receive messages, a process must have an identifier. What does that identifier include?
choices: Only the host's IP address
Only a port number
The host's IP address and a port number associated with the process
The host's name and the name of the application program
questions.explain: The IP address identifies the host. The port number identifies the process on that host. Together they identify the process.

questions.q: What is the well-known port number of an HTTP (web) server?
questions.explain: HTTP servers listen on port 80, so connecting to port 80 on a host reaches its web server.

questions.q: What is the well-known port number of a mail server (SMTP)?
questions.explain: Mail servers listen on port 25.

questions.q: How many bits long is the unique IP address of a host device, as described in this section (e.g., 128.119.245.12)?
questions.explain: Each host has a unique 32-bit IP address, written as four decimal numbers (8 bits each) separated by dots.

questions.q: If a host's IP address is like the street address of an apartment building, what plays the role of the apartment number?
choices: The host name, such as gaia.cs.umass.edu
The port number
The transport protocol, TCP or UDP
The application-layer protocol's message type
questions.explain: The IP address gets a message to the right host (the building). The port number picks the right process within that host (the apartment). A phone extension inside a company works the same way.

questions.q: To send an HTTP message to the web server on gaia.cs.umass.edu, what must the sender know?
choices: Only the server host's IP address
Only the port number 80
The server host's IP address and port number 25
The server host's IP address and port number 80
questions.explain: You need both parts of the process identifier: the host's IP address (128.119.245.12 in the example) and the web server's port, 80. Port 25 is the mail server port.

questions.q: Which of the following does an application-layer protocol define?
choices: The types of messages exchanged, e.g., request and response
Message syntax: what fields are in messages and how they are delineated
Message semantics: the meaning of the information in the fields
Rules for when and how processes send and respond to messages
The path that packets take through the routers of the network core
questions.explain: An application-layer protocol defines message types, syntax, semantics, and the rules for sending and responding. Routing through the network core belongs to the network layer, not the application-layer protocol.

questions.q: A protocol specification says each header line is a field name, a colon, and a value, ending with a carriage return and line feed. Which part of the protocol definition is this?
choices: Message syntax
Message semantics
Types of messages exchanged
Rules for when and how processes send and respond
questions.explain: Syntax covers what fields a message has and how the fields are delineated. It describes the format, not the meaning.

questions.q: A protocol specification says a status value of 1 in a response means the request succeeded, and 2 means the requested item does not exist. Which part of the protocol definition is this?
choices: Message syntax
Types of messages exchanged
Message semantics
Rules for when and how processes send and respond
questions.explain: Semantics is the meaning of the information in the fields, here what each status value means.

questions.q: A protocol specification says that after a client sends a request, the server must reply with exactly one response before the client sends another request. Which part of the protocol definition is this?
choices: Message syntax
Message semantics
Types of messages exchanged
Rules for when and how processes send and respond to messages
questions.explain: This specifies the actions processes take and the order of messages, so it belongs to the rules for when and how processes send and respond.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a proprietary application-layer protocol?
choices: HTTP
SMTP
The protocol used by Zoom
FTP
questions.explain: Zoom (and Skype) use proprietary protocols that a company owns and does not publish. HTTP, SMTP and FTP are open protocols defined in RFCs.

questions.q: What is a key benefit of open protocols such as HTTP and SMTP?
choices: They guarantee low delay for real-time applications
Their definitions are public, so independently written implementations can interoperate
They encrypt all data automatically
They need no transport-layer service
questions.explain: Open protocols are defined in publicly available RFCs. Because everyone can read the definition, anyone can implement the protocol, and their software will interoperate.

questions.q: Open Internet protocols such as HTTP and SMTP are specified in publicly available documents called RFCs. What does RFC stand for?
questions.explain: RFC = Request for Comments. For example, FTP is RFC 959 and SMTP is RFC 5321.

questions.q: A proprietary application-layer protocol's message syntax, semantics and rules are published in RFCs so anyone can implement it.
questions.explain: Proprietary protocols are usually owned by a company and their operation is not public. Only open protocols are published in RFCs.

questions.q: Which of the following are transport services an application might need?
choices: Data integrity (reliable data transfer)
Timing (low delay)
Throughput (a minimum rate)
Security (e.g., encryption, data integrity)
Choosing which routers in the network core carry its packets
questions.explain: The four needs are data integrity, timing, throughput and security. Routing decisions are made by the network layer and are not a transport service offered to applications.

questions.q: What is an elastic application?
choices: One that uses whatever throughput it gets
One that needs a minimum throughput to be effective
One that can tolerate some data loss
One that needs delays of only tens of milliseconds
questions.explain: Elastic apps (file transfer, email, web documents, text messaging) make use of whatever throughput is available. Multimedia apps instead need a minimum throughput to be effective.

questions.q: An application that needs a minimum amount of throughput to be effective, such as multimedia, is called an elastic application.
questions.explain: That describes a throughput-sensitive application. Elastic applications are the opposite: they use whatever throughput they get.

questions.q: In the transport-requirements table for common applications, which applications cannot tolerate data loss?
choices: File transfer/download
E-mail
Web documents
Real-time audio/video
Interactive games
Text messaging
questions.explain: File transfer, email, web documents and text messaging need no loss. Real-time and streaming audio/video and interactive games are loss-tolerant, because losing some packets only slightly degrades the experience.

questions.q: Which application is time-sensitive at the scale of a few seconds, rather than tens of milliseconds?
choices: Real-time audio/video
Streaming (stored) audio/video
Interactive games
File transfer
questions.explain: Streaming stored audio/video can buffer ahead, so a few seconds of delay is acceptable. Real-time audio/video and interactive games need delays in the tens of milliseconds. File transfer is not time-sensitive.

questions.q: Internet telephony and interactive games both need low delay to be effective. Which transport service need is this?
choices: Data integrity
Throughput
Timing
Security
questions.explain: Timing is the need for low delay from the sending process to the receiving process.

questions.q: A new app backs up a user's photo library to a server. Based on the requirements of similar apps (file transfer), which profile fits it best?
choices: Loss-tolerant, needs 10 Kbps-5 Mbps, time-sensitive to tens of milliseconds
Loss-tolerant, elastic, time-sensitive to a few seconds
No loss, needs a guaranteed minimum throughput, time-sensitive to tens of milliseconds
No loss, elastic, not time-sensitive
questions.explain: Like file transfer, a backup must arrive 100% intact, can use whatever throughput is available, and has no tight deadline.

questions.q: According to the requirements table, which profile fits an interactive multiplayer game?
choices: Loss-tolerant, needs Kbps+ of throughput, time-sensitive to tens of milliseconds
No loss, elastic, not time-sensitive
Loss-tolerant, elastic, time-sensitive to a few seconds
No loss, elastic, time-sensitive to tens of milliseconds
questions.explain: Interactive games tolerate some loss, need throughput on the order of Kbps and up, and need delays in the tens of milliseconds to feel responsive.

questions.q: Which application needs 100% reliable data transfer?
choices: Live Internet audio
Web transactions
Real-time video conferencing
Interactive games
questions.explain: Applications like file transfer and web transactions need 100% reliable data transfer. Audio and video can tolerate some loss.

questions.q: Which services does TCP provide?
choices: Reliable transport between sending and receiving processes
Flow control
Congestion control
Connection-oriented setup between client and server processes
A minimum throughput guarantee
Encryption of the data
questions.explain: TCP gives reliable transport, flow control, congestion control and connection setup. It does not provide timing, a minimum throughput guarantee, or security.

questions.q: A TCP sender holds back because the receiver's buffers are almost full. Which TCP service is at work?
choices: Congestion control
Flow control
Connection setup
Reliable transport
questions.explain: Flow control keeps the sender from overwhelming the receiver, so the sender doesn't send more than the receiver has buffer space for.

questions.q: A TCP sender slows down because the network between it and the receiver is overloaded. Which TCP service is at work?
choices: Flow control
Connection setup
Congestion control
Reliable transport
questions.explain: Congestion control throttles the sender when the network is overloaded. Flow control instead protects the receiver.

questions.q: What does it mean that TCP is connection-oriented?
choices: A dedicated physical circuit is reserved between the two hosts
Every packet takes the same path through the network
The connection guarantees a fixed delay
Setup (handshaking) between the client and server processes is required before data flows
questions.explain: Before data begins to flow, the client and server processes must do a setup handshake. UDP has no connection setup.

questions.q: Which describes UDP's service?
choices: Unreliable data transfer between sending and receiving processes, with no flow control, congestion control or connection setup
Reliable data transfer with flow control but no congestion control
Connection-oriented transfer with a guaranteed minimum throughput
Encrypted transfer with end-point authentication
questions.explain: UDP offers only best-effort, unreliable data transfer between processes. It provides no reliability, flow control, congestion control, timing, throughput guarantee, security or connection setup.

questions.q: UDP provides even fewer services than TCP. Why is it still useful?
choices: UDP guarantees lower delay than TCP
UDP encrypts data, which TCP does not
An application can build just the extra services it needs on top of UDP, in the application layer
UDP is required by all client-server applications
questions.explain: Applications can add whatever services they need on top of UDP in the application layer, without TCP's built-in behavior. UDP itself gives no timing guarantee and no security.

questions.q: Which of these services does neither TCP nor UDP provide?
choices: Reliable delivery
Flow control
Congestion control
A minimum throughput guarantee
questions.explain: Neither Internet transport protocol guarantees timing, minimum throughput or security. TCP provides reliable delivery, flow control and congestion control. UDP provides none of them.

questions.q: In the table of Internet applications and their transport protocols, which applications may run over UDP?
choices: File transfer (FTP)
E-mail (SMTP)
Web documents (HTTP)
Internet telephony (SIP, RTP, or proprietary)
Interactive games (e.g., WOW, FPS, proprietary)
questions.explain: FTP, SMTP and HTTP use TCP because they need reliable transfer. Internet telephony uses TCP or UDP, and interactive games use UDP or TCP.

questions.q: Streaming audio/video using HTTP and DASH runs over TCP, even though streaming media can tolerate some loss.
questions.explain: The table lists streaming audio/video (HTTP, DASH) over TCP. Overall, TCP is by far the most widely used transport service.

questions.q: Which transport protocol should a file transfer application use, and why?
choices: UDP, because file transfer is time-sensitive
TCP, because file transfer needs 100% reliable data transfer
UDP, because file transfer needs a minimum throughput guarantee
TCP, because TCP guarantees low delay
questions.explain: File transfer cannot tolerate loss, so it uses TCP's reliable transport (FTP runs over TCP). TCP gives no delay or throughput guarantees, and file transfer is elastic and not time-sensitive anyway.

questions.q: Plain (vanilla) TCP and UDP sockets encrypt data, so a password sent into a socket is protected as it crosses the Internet.
questions.explain: Vanilla TCP and UDP sockets do no encryption. A cleartext password sent into the socket crosses the Internet in cleartext. The original 1980s socket abstraction had no security concepts, so applications had to build security in themselves.

questions.q: Which services does Transport Layer Security (TLS) provide?
choices: Encrypted TCP connections
Data integrity
End-point authentication
A guaranteed minimum throughput
Low-delay timing guarantees
questions.explain: TLS provides encryption, data integrity and end-point authentication over TCP. It adds no timing or throughput guarantees.

questions.q: Where is TLS implemented?
choices: In the network core, where routers encrypt packets as they forward them
In the operating system's UDP implementation
In the application layer: apps use TLS libraries, which in turn use TCP
In the physical layer, by scrambling signals on each link
questions.explain: TLS is a shim implemented in application (user) space on top of TCP sockets. Applications call TLS libraries, and those libraries use TCP.

questions.q: An application using TLS writes a password in cleartext into its TLS socket. How does the password cross the Internet?
choices: Encrypted
In cleartext, because the application did not encrypt it itself
Encrypted only if UDP is used underneath
It is never sent, because TLS refuses to carry passwords
questions.explain: With TLS, cleartext sent into the socket crosses the Internet encrypted. The TLS layer does the encryption for the application.

questions.q: What does TLS stand for?
questions.explain: TLS = Transport Layer Security. It provides encrypted TCP connections with data integrity and end-point authentication.

questions.q: What does end-point authentication mean?
choices: Proving to the other side that you are who you say you are
Making sure the data was not changed in transit
Hiding the contents of messages from eavesdroppers
Guaranteeing that the other side has enough buffer space
questions.explain: End-point authentication lets each side verify the other's identity. Detecting changes is data integrity, hiding contents is encryption, and buffer space is TCP flow control.
